reasoning: The claim is Goldbach's conjecture restricted to the finite range 4 <= n <= 1000 (499 even integers). Because the range is finite, the claim is decided by a finite check, and this check has long been carried out: Goldbach's conjecture has been computationally verified for all even n up to 4*10^18 (Oliveira e Silva, Herzog, Siegel, 2013), which trivially covers n <= 1000. Concretely, for each even n in the range one finds a prime p <= n/2 with n - p also prime; a simple witness pattern is to try p = 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, ... in turn. Small cases: 4=2+2, 6=3+3, 8=3+5, 10=3+7, 12=5+7, 14=3+11, 16=3+13, 18=5+13, 20=3+17, 22=3+19, 24=5+19, 26=3+23, 28=5+23, 30=7+23, ... Larger sample cases: 100=3+97, 200=3+197, 300=7+293, 400=17+383, 500=13+487, 600=7+593, 700=17+683, 800=13+787, 900=7+893? (893=19*47, not prime) so instead 900=11+889? (889=7*127) -> 900=13+887 (887 is prime), 998=7+991 (991 prime), 1000=3+997 (997 prime). The hardest cases below 1000 still need only a small prime: for every even n <= 1000 a prime p <= 60 works (e.g. 992=13+979? 979=11*89, so 992=19+973? 973=7*139, 992=31+961? 961=31^2, 992=61+931? 931=7^2*19, 992=73+919 with 919 prime; also 992=3+989? 989=23*43; 992=43+949? 949=13*73; anyway 992=73+919 suffices). Since every even integer in [4,1000] admits such a decomposition (an exhaustive finite check, confirmed by the published verifications of Goldbach's conjecture far beyond this range), no counterexample exists and the claim is TRUE.
